title: Vec and Ownership
story: A Vec is a container that owns everything inside it. When you move the Vec, every element moves too. When you borrow the Vec, you can inspect its contents.
why: Vec is the most common collection type in XIOM — understanding how ownership works with collections is fundamental to writing real programs.
analogy: A Vec is like a bookshelf — the shelf owns the books on it. You can look at books (&), rearrange them (&mut), or move the entire shelf to a new room.
try_it: Write a function that takes &mut Vec[Int] and reverses the elements in place. Test it with multiple Vecs of different sizes.
tips: Vec[T] owns every T in it — moving the Vec moves all elements
Use &Vec[T] to iterate and inspect, &mut Vec[T] to modify elements
Accessing vec[i] through a borrow gives you a reference, not ownership
Vec operations like push/pop require &mut — they modify the Vec
common_mistakes: Trying to iterate (&) and push (&mut) at the same time — borrow conflict
Assuming cloning a Vec clones its elements — it clones the Vec structure AND elements
Forgetting that moving a Vec out of a struct moves the struct's field
